analysis.one_liner: Bars dominant app stores from forcing developers to use their payment systems and locks out rival stores.
analysis.headline: The Open App Markets Act, reintroduced with bipartisan sponsorship in June 2025, sits untouched in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no action beyond referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets the two companies that control the phone app stores most Americans use. It would forbid them from forcing app makers to use their payment systems, which currently take a cut of up to 30% of many in-app purchases, and would require them to let people install apps and rival app stores from outside their official stores. It would also stop the store owner from secretly using data about a competitor's app to build a competing one, and from ranking its own apps above rivals in search results. Enforcement would fall to the FTC, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and app developers themselves, who could sue for triple damages.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers and their customers. Developers keep a bigger share of what users pay them and get new ways to reach customers, such as telling users about cheaper prices on their own website. Consumers get more places to buy apps, potentially lower prices, and the ability to delete preinstalled apps. Smaller app stores and payment companies gain the right to compete on iPhones and Android phones.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered companies (those running an app store with more than 50 million U.S. users that also control the operating system) from requiring developers to use their in-app payment system as a condition of distribution [S2].
Requires the store owner to let users set third-party apps and app stores as defaults, install them outside the official store, and hide or delete preinstalled apps [S2].
Bars using nonpublic data collected about a developer's app to compete with that app, and bars unreasonably ranking the company's own apps above rivals in store search results [S2].
Lets developers communicate directly with their users about prices and offers, and gives developers injured by violations the right to sue for threefold damages plus attorney's fees [S2].
Gives the FTC independent litigation authority to bring its own civil actions, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, whose app stores would lose much of their power to take a percentage of in-app purchases and to channel all app distribution through their own stores. Their revenue from app store commissions and their control over which apps phone users can install would shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apple's and Google's app store businesses

drawbacks.text: Allowing installation of apps and app stores from outside the official stores raises real fraud and security risks; the bill responds with a privacy-and-security exception but only enforces it if the company proves, by a preponderance of the evidence, that restrictions are consistent and narrowly tailored, which could mean years of litigation over each case [S2].
The bill makes the store owner certify under penalty of perjury that security actions are not pretextual, adding legal exposure that companies say could make them over-restrict apps to be safe [S2].

Critics of the approach argue that breaking the single-store model benefits large developers with their own customer bases more than small ones, since big companies can more easily run their own distribution and payments [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is money: cutting the mandatory commission on in-app purchases and opening distribution would lower costs for developers, some of which would likely reach consumers through lower prices, and users would gain real choice over what they install. The main cost is a genuine one: the curated, single-store model is part of how phones stay safe from malware, and opening it up will lead to some fraud and disputes over what security measures are legitimate. The bill tries to manage that with a security exception, but its effectiveness depends on how courts apply it. On balance the bill shifts money and control from two very large companies toward developers and consumers, with a manageable but real security trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2025, and nothing has happened to it since; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on June 24, 2025, joined by Senators Blumenthal, Lee, Klobuchar, and Durbin [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
The committee has taken no further recorded action; there are no markup, hearing, or vote entries in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google, whose app store businesses face no new restrictions while the bill waits in committee; the companies have spent heavily lobbying against earlier versions of this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Apple and Google's app store status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely mixed: a Republican lead sponsor with three Democrats and one additional Republican cosigning the same bill.

industries.industry: Mobile app stores (Apple App Store, Google Play)
industries.note: The bill strips the two dominant stores of their power to require their own payment systems and take a cut of in-app purchases, and to be the only channel for installing apps. Their gain has come from charging developers up to 30% on purchases, a cost passed into app prices and subscriptions that consumers pay.

Beyond payments, the bill forces the operating system owners to allow rival app stores, sideloading, deletion of preinstalled apps, and equal access to system interfaces, reducing their control over the phone itself.
Developers keep more of their revenue, gain direct customer communication and alternative distribution, and can sue for treble damages when the rules are violated.

industries.industry: Third-party app stores and alternative payment providers
industries.note: Companies currently barred or heavily restricted from distributing apps or processing payments on iPhones and Android would be allowed to compete.

analysis.trajectory: This is the third Congress in a row an Open App Markets Act has been introduced. Earlier versions advanced through Senate Judiciary but never reached the floor. With the bill sitting in committee with no scheduled action and opposition from two of the most well-resourced lobby operations in Washington, the realistic path is a possible committee hearing at best and, more likely, no floor vote before the Congress ends.
